findings.location: sections/30-son-and-lord-of-david.tex, subsection 'The other texts as confession', the Alleluia paragraph (PDF p. 23): 'In the same place he makes a distinction that belongs to this reading. Christ and the Church are one, sed Verbum et caro non utrumque unum; Pater et Verbum utrumque unum: the Word and the flesh are not one thing, while the Father and the Word are one (Enarrationes in Psalmos 101, s. 1, 2).'
findings.problem: The English gloss drops the whole of Augustine's distinction and leaves a sentence that, read plainly, denies the unity of the Incarnation. I read the Latin at the locus the study cites (augustinus.it, In Psalmum 101 enarratio I, sect. 2). Augustine writes: 'Christus et Ecclesia, utrumque unus: sed Verbum et caro non utrumque unum; Pater et Verbum utrumque unum; Christus et Ecclesia utrumque unus, unus quidam vir perfectus.' The antithesis is carried entirely by the gender of the pronoun. Christ and the Church are one man, masculine unus; the Father and the Word are one thing, neuter unum, that is one in substance; and the Word and the flesh are not one thing in that sense, though they are one person -- which is why Augustine can say in the same breath that Christ and the Church are unus. English cannot carry the point by gender, and the study supplies nothing in its place: it renders one member 'are not one thing' and the next 'are one', and it quotes only the two neuter members, dropping the masculine one that the study's own first reading quotes nine pages earlier ('Christus et Ecclesia utrumque unus ... unus quidam vir perfectus', sections/20-whole-heart-one-body.tex, PDF p. 17). The 'sed' is then left with nothing to turn on, and what reaches the reader is the bare proposition that the Word and the flesh are not one. That proposition stands in the one reading whose subject is that Christ is David's son according to the flesh and David's Lord according to his eternal birth, three paragraphs after the study has told the reader that 'the Word deigned to take our death' and a page before it quotes the Preface on 'a Trinity of one substance'; a reader who takes the sentence at its word has been given, in a study of unusual doctrinal care, an unqualified denial of what Chalcedon affirms of the one person. The Latin is transcribed accurately and the evidence behind it is sound; the defect is the study's presentation of it, and it is the only place in the three readings where the prose says something its source does not mean.
findings.required_result: No sentence of the study states without qualification that the Word and the flesh are not one. Either the gloss says what Augustine's antithesis actually distinguishes -- that the Father and the Word are one in substance, while the Word and the flesh, one person, are not one substance -- or the quotation is restored to include the masculine member of Augustine's own sentence ('Christus et Ecclesia utrumque unus ... unus quidam vir perfectus', already quoted in sections/20) so that the unus/unum contrast is visible to the reader, with the English making the contrast explicit. The locus remains Enarrationes in Psalmos 101, s. 1, 2, and research/interpretations.md section 2.3 should carry the clause the reading uses, as research/scope.md section 3.5 already carries the rest of the sentence.

findings.location: research/interpretations.md section 3 (3.2 'Principal witnesses and their reasoning', the 3.3 element table's Offertory row, the 3.4 moral sense, and the lane's row in 'The three readings in brief'), against proper-components.toml [[lanes]] key = 'just-judge-merciful-hearer' and sections/40-just-judge-merciful-hearer.tex, 'Daniel's prayer and Daniel's people' (PDF p. 27) and that reading's moral sense (PDF p. 30)
findings.problem: Standing advisory from study-review iterations 0, 2, 3, 4 and 5, still uncleared at iteration 6 and restated because this stage's entries replace its previous ones in evaluations/blocking-findings-v1.toml. It stays advisory: the severity was decided when the defect was first seen and does not change because the round has come round again. proper-components.toml declares Thomas Aquinas among the just-judge-merciful-hearer lane's authors, and sections/40 develops him there -- 'prayer must be made with confidence of obtaining, and that confidence comes from God's mercy' (Super Philippenses c. 4, on 4:6, using Dan 9:18) -- and credits him by name in that reading's moral sense. research/interpretations.md section 3 names him at none of its four loci; I read the whole section in its sealed bytes and 'Aquinas' does not occur in it. The evidence is sound and independently checked: research/scope.md 3.7 records the locus, the Dessain 1857 vol. 2 p. 398 page image read, and exactly the source role the study uses ('Aquinas uses Dan 9:18 as doctrine on prayer; he does not expound Daniel'). The same section's 'three readings in brief' row for this lane also omits John Chrysostom, whom the manifest declares and whom section 3.2 and the 3.3 Epistle row both carry, so the summary row is narrower than the section it summarises as well as narrower than the manifest. What iteration 6 repaired was STU-013, the generation-metadata declaration that wrongly reported this cleared; no record of the leaf now claims the repair has been made, and the author correctly declined to edit a reviewed upstream record from the study stage. No reader of the PDF meets a false claim; what is broken is the correspondence between the manifest, the interpretation audit and the section, which those records exist to make inspectable.
findings.required_result: research/interpretations.md section 3 records Thomas Aquinas among the just-judge-merciful-hearer reading's witnesses, with his locus (Super Philippenses c. 4, on 4:6) and the source role research/scope.md 3.7 gives him, and his name in the 3.3 Offertory row, the 3.4 moral sense and the lane's row in 'The three readings in brief'; that same summary row also names John Chrysostom, whom 3.2 and the 3.3 Epistle row already carry. Its owner is the research stage, whose file this is. Until that owner does it, no record of the leaf may state that it has been done.

observations.location: sections/90-apparatus.tex, References: the entries for St Augustine (Enarrationes in Psalmos, 'on Ps 32, I, 6, 12, and II, s. 2, 5, 8, 15-18'), Rupert of Deutz (De divinis officiis XII.17-18) and St Robert Bellarmine (on Pss 32:6, 12; 75:9-13; 101:2; 118:1, 124, 137) (PDF pp. 37-38)
observations.note: Three reference loci reach past what the study actually cites, one more than the last round recorded. The body uses Augustine on Ps 32 at I, 12 and at II, s. 2, 5 and II, s. 2, 15-18, but nowhere at I, 6 or at II, s. 2, 8; it uses Rupert at XII.17 only, XII.18 reaching no claim; and it uses Bellarmine on Ps 32:6 and 12, Ps 75, Ps 101:2 and Ps 118:124 and 137, but nowhere on Ps 118:1, which research/scope.md 3.1 records as read. Each is one item wider than the claims it supports rather than an unused source, which is ordinary scholarly latitude and does not reach my criteria as a finding; I record it because a reader checking the apparatus against the body will find the mismatch, and because the count has grown by one while the observation has stood.

observations.location: sections/80-date-location.tex, the Date column of the Gospel dossier ('Event - No narrated-event date in the chronology corpus') and of the Offertory dossier ('Historical setting: Duration: all these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years') (PDF pp. 33-34)
observations.note: Two of the seven Date cells report a state of the chronology corpus rather than a date. The Gospel's narrated event -- the controversy in the Temple, which the Location cell dates by nothing but Mt 21:23 -- has no date in the corpus and says so; the Offertory's historical-setting group prints a duration quoted from Jeremias instead of a date for the prayer in the first year of Darius the Mede that the same dossier's Location cell identifies. Both are exactly what research/chronology-annotations.tex generates, the study is forbidden to hand-author over them, and sections/90-apparatus.tex discloses the limit honestly, so this is not a defect of the study. I record it because these two cells are carried unchanged into the concise companion's physical page 2, where the Date column is the point of the sheet, and because the gap is in the shared chronology corpus rather than in this leaf -- a reader of page 2 will ask why the Gospel's event carries no date at all.

summary: Independent cold review of the expansive study src/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/1962/propers/temporal/57-seventeenth-after-pentecost/main.tex with all nine section components, read whole against guidance/liturgy/propers-three-documents.md and the 1962 profile, and against the leaf's own evidence (propers/verified.md, research/context.md, research/scope.md, research/interpretations.md, research/chronology-annotations.tex). The packet seal was verified first: all nineteen files named in REVIEW_INPUTS hash exactly as stated. The built artifact build/tpt-runs/1e02dc05f2df9940/artifacts/author-study-0006/57-seventeenth-after-pentecost.pdf is 38 physical pages, inside the 20-50 contract, and carries the Scriptural Date and Location dossiers the concise opening needs (pp. 33-34) with every Date cell coming from the generated chronology annotations. Three readings are developed, each distinguishable in anchor, governing emphasis and consequence, each engaging the whole formulary, each carrying its own four senses with a literal row that is literal and an anagogical row that is eschatological, and each drawing developed reasoning from well more than two Fathers or saints; the comparison is a real comparison and preserves the narrow disagreements (Augustine against Cassiodorus on Ps 101, Augustine against Jerome on Daniel's own sins, Jerome and Aquinas against Chrysostom and Theodoret on Eph 4:6, Hilary against Augustine on where mercy begins, Bellarmine against Rupert and Durandus on iudicium). Source roles are honest: Gregory is said to expound Mt 22:1-13 and cite the commandment from Mark, Irenaeus to use Ps 32:6 as a proof text and not expound the psalm, Rupert and Durandus to read this office with Luke 14, and reading 2 says outright where the Offertory's Christological weight lies outside the sung verses. Checked independently against the sources themselves, not against the records: Chrysostom In Mt. hom. 71 and In Eph. hom. 9-11 (NPNF via NewAdvent), Augustine De doctrina christiana I.22, I.27, I.30 and the Latin of En. in Ps. 101 s. 1, 2 (augustinus.it), Basil De Spiritu Sancto 16.38, Irenaeus Adv. haer. I.22.1, Aquinas Super Mt. c. 22 lect. 4 and Super Psalmos 32 nn. 5 and 11 (Corpus Thomisticum), eight Bellarmine passages (O'Sullivan, eCatholic2000), Gueranger's account of the day's name and of Tomasi's antiphonary (Liturgical Year XI, archive.org), and Wilson's Gelasian at Liber III sect. XIII and appendix p. 359 for the Collect's older te solum Dominum puro corde and the three orations at Hebd. xxi. Every one of those matched the study word for word; I found no false attribution, no invented consensus and no unevidenced claim of compositional intent. Meaningful limits of this review: I did not re-read the Missal facsimile, Jerome in PL 25 and 26, Theodoret's and Chrysostom's Greek, Hilary's CSEL pages, Cassiodorus at monumenta.ch, Schuster, Durandus, Rupert or Wilson's Gregorian on their page images, and for those I checked the leaf's records for internal consistency rather than re-deriving them. One blocking defect remains, and it is in the study's presentation of a source it quotes correctly: the gloss on Augustine's Verbum et caro antithesis in the second reading. STU-006 is restated as the standing advisory it has been since iteration 0 and is still uncleared; STU-014 and STU-015 are cleared and are not restated.
